titulo: Reduced Relatives, Participle Clauses and Nominalisation
descripcion: The density that separates C1 writing from B2 writing comes from three devices working together: dropping the relative pronoun, compressing a clause into a participle, and turning a verb into a noun. Used separately, each one saves a few words. Used together in the same paragraph, they produce the compact, confident register of a strong report.

cuadroReferencia.notaPie: Combining all three in one sentence is normal in a report; combining them in speech reads as stiff. Match the density to the register.

ejemplos.texto: Having been delayed twice, the report published last week drew immediate criticism.
The team's quick decision, taken under pressure, avoided a bigger loss.
Data collected over three years, though incomplete, still points the same way.

notas: A reduced relative only works when the missing pronoun would have been the subject; the report I read cannot become the report read by me here.
Nominalising every verb in a paragraph makes it unreadable; alternate nominal and verbal sentences.
A dangling participle is the most common failure of this combination: the participle's implied subject must match the main clause's subject.

contraste.es: Spanish tolerates an implicit, ambiguous subject in gerund constructions much better (estando en Madrid, me llamaron), while English requires the subject of the participle to match that of the main clause. Spanish speakers produce dangling participles precisely because the construction is acceptable in Spanish.
contraste.de: German nominalises readily, so the nominalisation part of this cluster is easy for German speakers. The difference lies in the reduced relative, which English places after the noun where German uses a prenominal participle phrase, and in keeping participle clauses tied to the subject of the main clause.
contraste.it: Postnominal participles are native to Italian, and bureaucratic Italian nominalises heavily, so two of the three devices come easily. The risk is the dangling participle or gerund, which colloquial Italian tolerates much more than written English.
contraste.fr: Formal French nominalises readily and uses postnominal participles, and French speakers know the same-subject rule for the gérondif. This cluster is therefore relatively easy for them; the main risk is over-compressing texts in genres where English prefers a verbal style.
contraste.pt: Postnominal participles are native to Portuguese, but the personal infinitive lets Portuguese stay verbal where English nominalises. Portuguese speakers therefore tend to under-nominalise and, especially in Brazilian usage, to produce dangling gerund clauses.

errores: Producing a dangling participle where the implied subject doesn't match the main clause.
Reducing a relative clause where the missing pronoun would be the object, which isn't grammatically allowed.
Nominalising every sentence in a row until the paragraph becomes unreadable.
autochequeo: Is the reduced pronoun always the subject, never the object, of its clause?
Does every participle's implied subject match the main clause's subject?
Is the paragraph a mix of nominal and verbal sentences, not all one or the other?
Would the density fit a spoken conversation, or does it belong only in writing?
Is at least one dangling participle risk checked and fixed?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on reduced relatives, participle clauses and nominalisation. Flag every dangling participle, check whether reductions are grammatically allowed, and say whether the density fits the register. Do not rewrite the text.
